# Decision history — akr

Every revision of every decision, plus the terminal revisions of other normative records. Includes archived records: this is the project's memory of what it used to think.

## akr.decision.change-transaction-not-commit-kind

### Revision 3 — AKR leads intent, git seals the snapshot, and the bridge is a change transaction

`active` · `@akr.decision.change-transaction-not-commit-kind/3` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/change.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/change/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/git/**"`, `path "docs/16-change-protocol.md"`

No new record kind. The bridge is AKR work record -> local change transaction -> staged git tree -> generated or explicitly reworded commit prose -> canonical trailers. The transaction lives at `$(git rev-parse --git-path akr/current-change.akr)`: local to the worktree, safe to discard, absent from search and context, never committed. The staged tree, not the working tree, is the synchronisation boundary. `akr diff --staged` computes a semantic delta by parsing the HEAD ledger and the index ledger and comparing them, never `git diff` text, so a reformat or reorder is not a semantic change. `akr change prepare --staged` refuses a material code change that names neither a work record nor an explicit `--untracked-reason`, and records the staged tree id so a tree that moves afterwards invalidates the preparation. `akr git commit` generates the message and hands the index to git; repeated `-m`/`--message` values may replace the human subject and body, but the bridge always retains its canonical trailers. AKR does not implement an object store. The durable link is commit trailers -- AKR-Change, AKR-Work, AKR-Evidence, AKR-Decision, AKR-Graph, AKR-Tree -- which point from the commit to the records, survive rebases and cherry-picks, and can be rebuilt by walking history. Evidence names the code it verified through an implementation digest over the staged tree's sorted (path, mode, blob) triples, excluding `.akr/**` and `docs/generated/**`, which breaks the cycle of the digest changing when the digest is written down. A commit still never completes work; the transaction consumes AKR state transitions and never invents them.

**Context.** An agent finished and verified a substantial change while every corresponding work record still said proposed. A later check caught the divergence, but only because someone ran it. Tooling should make the synchronised path easier than the unsynchronised one -- the question was whether that needs a `commit` record kind.

**Consequences.** A durable `commit` kind was rejected: one work record takes many commits, one commit advances several work records, rebasing changes every object id, and a commit hash cannot be written into a file contained in that same commit without an amendment loop. Hooks were considered as the primary mechanism and rejected as the primary mechanism too, since they are bypassable; `akr git install-hooks` writes thin wrappers around `akr git-hook`, which runs the same verification an author can run by hand, and CI remains the final authority.

**supersedes** `@akr.decision.change-transaction-not-commit-kind/2`

## akr.decision.completed-planning-work-satisfies-dependency

### Revision 1 — Completed planning work satisfies a dependency

`active` · `@akr.decision.completed-planning-work-satisfies-dependency/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-core/src/validate/**"`, `path "docs/02-data-model.md"`, `path "docs/04-references-and-versioning.md"`, `path "docs/05-validation-rules.md"`, `path "docs/06-compiler-pipeline.md"`, `path "docs/10-freshness-and-git.md"`, `path "spec/**"`

A completed planning record satisfies a depends_on prerequisite. Both pinned and floating depends_on references may therefore retain a completed target; abandonment, supersession, rejection, withdrawal, and disproof remain invalid dependency outcomes. Completion must preserve the edge as provenance instead of forcing a bookkeeping revision that deletes the milestone chain. Recorded as D-035.

## akr.decision.compress-state-not-search

### Revision 1 — Compress the state, not the search: an advisor packet has two layers and one is withheld

`proposed` · `@akr.decision.compress-state-not-search/1` · scope `all`

Handing a task to a second model produces an advisor packet, not a summary. A packet carries two typed layers. Layer A is administrative fact: the user's request verbatim, HEAD and its subject, the ledger revision, dirty paths with digests, the session head, declared namespaces, the governing goal and records, the search envelope, commands with what they produced, baselines, constraints, evidence and artefacts. All of it may be compressed. Layer B is worker interpretation: hypotheses, what was examined, what was not examined, proposed approaches, searches already run. It may be recorded and may not be substituted for the problem. handoff open renders Layer A and reports only that Layer B exists; handoff reveal releases it and stamps the packet, so whether a review was independent is knowable afterwards. The task field is verbatim, the search envelope defaults to the whole project, and the workspace is fingerprinted by HEAD, the source-graph hash and a sha256 per dirty path so that open and verify report exact or drifted and name what moved. Packets live in .agent/handoffs/, gitignored, invisible to search, context and the compiler, and are never records. Recorded as D-040.

**Context.** An agent doing the work reaches a point where a second model would help, and the obvious handoff is a summary of what it found. That destroys the reason for making it: if the advisor's value is finding what the first agent missed, a summary of what the first agent noticed makes it a perceptual bottleneck, and its blind spot silently becomes the advisor's boundary. Afterwards nobody can tell, because a narrowed task reads exactly like a narrow one. The opposite failure was measured too: an advisor arriving cold spends its most expensive tokens on questions with deterministic answers, and in one logged run had to discover and correct the base_rev requirement mid-task. Both failures are the same mistake in opposite directions.

**Consequences.** .agent/ now has two ignored subtrees rather than the one D-036 settled on; that line of D-036 was reasoning about the .agents/ versus .agent/ collision, which a second subtree under the same name does not reintroduce. The MCP Tool::writes field widens from writes to .akr/records/ to changes the workspace, because readOnlyHint and --surface read both read it and both would be lying if a tool that created a packet reported itself read-only; a third runner, run_coordination, sits beside run_read and run_write. knowledge.handoff_open carries the largest budget on the surface, and because a packet is addressable its overflow path names knowledge.handoff_expand rather than truncating everything. There is deliberately no reveal-on-open argument over MCP where the command line has --reveal: the CLI flag is one process and one recorded act, an MCP flag would make a read-only tool write, and the one-implementation invariant still holds because akr handoff open reproduces knowledge.handoff_open exactly. AKR does not become a model orchestrator: it owns state, context, packet construction, retrieval, provenance and snapshot verification, and a packet is provider-neutral.

## akr.decision.dirty-source-graph-has-no-commit-provenance

### Revision 1 — Dirty source graphs do not claim HEAD provenance

`proposed` · `@akr.decision.dirty-source-graph-has-no-commit-provenance/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/session.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/store/**"`, `path "docs/06-compiler-pipeline.md"`, `path "docs/07-cli.md"`

The source-graph hash is the exact identity of the AKR bytes a command read. The Git commit is attached only when those loaded AKR sources match the committed tree. A mid-flight build may still write rebuildable caches, the lock, and views from dirty AKR sources, but their commit provenance is absent rather than naming the pre-change HEAD. Freshness may still use HEAD as its history boundary; source provenance and history comparison are separate facts.

## akr.decision.durable-evidence-artifact

### Revision 2 — A cited artefact must outlive the citation, and that is a rule rather than a flag check

`active` · `@akr.decision.durable-evidence-artifact/2` · scope `all`

An evidence record's artifact slot may not name a path under an unkept .agent/scratch entry. This is V-025, raising AKR-T023 at type-check over the model, not a guard on akr evidence add --artifact. The keep index is attached as a workspace fact on both read and write pipelines, so an entry protected by akr scratch keep is persistent and valid on all four evidence write routes; an unkept entry is refused before anything is written. The comparison is textual and normalises separators, a leading ./ and an absolute path passing through a scratch directory, and it reads the artifact slot only. Recorded as D-037 and clarified after field verification of the documented keep escape hatch.

**Context.** Scratch is the one directory the protocol documents as disposable, and akr scratch prune empties it on an ordinary handoff. An artefact cited from there is a verified claim whose backing a later session removes without knowing it was cited, and nothing notices, because a path is not a reference the ledger resolves. The audit behind the scratch-lifecycle work found 38 records across five files citing scratch paths, most already dangling. The first fix put the refusal in front of one flag; a review of the change found that three of the four write routes never reach that flag.

**Consequences.** A ledger that already cites scratch artefacts fails akr check until those records are revised, including on the next unrelated write, because the write pipeline validates the whole resulting ledger. That is the intended forcing function and the same standing every other V-rule has, but it is a real migration cost for the workspaces the original audit was about; akr scratch keep <entry> is the escape hatch for an artefact that should stay where it is. This does not re-open the scratch-lifecycle ruling that scratch is never a ledger diagnostic: that is about the directory's contents, how much is sitting there and how old, which akr check reports as a build fact. V-025 is about a record, and the record is wrong whether or not the file behind it still exists.

**supersedes** `@akr.decision.durable-evidence-artifact/1`

## akr.decision.executable-authoring-contracts

### Revision 3 — Authoring and transport contracts are executable

`active` · `@akr.decision.executable-authoring-contracts/3` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/freshness/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/validate/**"`, `path "crates/akr-mcp/**"`, `path "docs/**"`, `path "scripts/setup-akr-mcp.*"`, `path "spec/**"`

AKR authoring surfaces must expose typed per-kind slots, legal relations, canonical reference forms, and an executable recovery step before or with a rejected write. The MCP schema derives each kind's exact required and optional slots from the vocabulary, exposes scope as compact strings or a closed oneOf of typed forms, and rejects topic on non-normative kinds before ledger validation. Line-only source citations normalize trailing blank end lines to the same byte and line convention AKR-S022 validates. Generic slot serialization follows the vocabulary value type on both propose and revise, including carrying a collated papercut's string-array dedup set. Scope globs matching no tracked path remain non-fatal authoring warnings. Successful MCP writes name the required build step. MCP reliability is verified through a long-lived installed subprocess running mixed successful and rejected calls, while setup verifies the installed binary and tells clients to reconnect after replacement.

**Context.** Repeated papercuts were caused less by missing capability than by contracts that became visible only after a failed call, plus transport reports not covered by in-memory tests.

**Consequences.** Help, schemas, diagnostics, and write responses duplicate a small amount of generated vocabulary for discoverability. Transport coverage costs additional test time but exercises the connector boundary users actually run.

**supersedes** `@akr.decision.executable-authoring-contracts/2`

## akr.decision.external-sources-immutable-library

### Revision 2 — External sources are immutable while registered and explicitly finalizable

`proposed` · `@akr.decision.external-sources-immutable-library/2` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/source.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/source/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/store/sources.rs"`, `path "docs/15-external-sources.md"`, `path "sources/**"`, `path "spec/schema/sources.sql"`

Outside advice is held in three layers with one responsibility each. The source library is non-authoritative and content-hashed: registered bytes are immutable while present, but registration is not permanent. `akr source add` copies a document under `sources/external/` and creates no records. `akr source finalize` can transition a document from `full` to `cited-only`, retaining exact cited ranges in shared content-addressed `.akr/source-fragments/` blobs, or to `metadata-only` when no exact citations remain. The catalog tombstone retains title, origin, identity and the full document hash; the original Markdown may leave the active source tree.

The derived source index, `.akr/cache/sources.sqlite`, holds rebuildable, non-authoritative semantic chunks on its own generation, distinct from the ledger's `source_graph_hash`. Full sources are searchable; finalized fragments are explicit provenance, not ordinary project search results. The ledger holds the project's interpretation: records cite a document and exact byte range, optionally with a role and `use` note explaining what the project adopted. Both CLI authoring and `knowledge.propose`/`knowledge.revise` must accept that exact locator; registration without an explicit adoption path is not a plan import. A record must remain semantically self-contained when its provenance blocks are hidden. `akr check` resolves exact citations from the full document or retained fragments and refuses a citation whose bytes are unavailable. Lineage-only references are valid in `metadata-only` state.

Finalization does not rewrite records, duplicate excerpts into them, change a work state, satisfy evidence, or imply that outside advice was implemented. It is a source retention transition, separate from provenance interpretation and work completion.

**Context.** The first source-library design made registered Markdown permanently undeletable in order to preserve exact citations. Use across multiple projects showed that advisor reports are often temporary intake documents, while the exact passages that records cite still need portable provenance. Literal absorption into every record would create revision noise and duplicate overlapping prose, so shared retained fragments preserve exact resolution without making ordinary context packets larger.

**Consequences.** Source cleanup is explicit and inspectable through `source status`, `source dependents` and `source finalize --dry-run`. Full documents remain appropriate for standards and references that may yield future records; cited-only is the normal final state for advisor reports; metadata-only is permitted only for lineage references. A missing full source is an error, a missing retained fragment is an error, and a metadata-only exact citation is an error. Git history may retain the removed Markdown, but portable AKR fragments do not depend on that history.

**supersedes** `@akr.decision.external-sources-immutable-library/1`

### Revision 1 — External sources are an immutable library, indexed separately, cited by byte range

`superseded` · `@akr.decision.external-sources-immutable-library/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/source.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/source/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/store/sources.rs"`, `path "docs/15-external-sources.md"`, `path "sources/**"`, `path "spec/schema/sources.sql"`

Outside advice is held in three layers with one responsibility each. The immutable
source library, `sources/`, holds exact outside bytes: `akr source add` content-hashes
a document, copies it under `sources/external/`, and adds a catalog entry, creating no
records; editing a registered file is AKR-S021 from both `akr source verify` and
`akr check`, and the only correction is registering a superseding version. The derived
source index, `.akr/cache/sources.sqlite`, holds rebuildable, non-authoritative semantic
chunks — heading paths, byte and line ranges, normalised search text, expanded technical
symbols, ranked by BM25 — on its own generation, `source_corpus_hash`, distinct from the
ledger's `source_graph_hash`, so a record write never rechunks the corpus and a
registration never re-resolves the ledger. The ledger holds only the project's
interpretation: records cite the library through a `source` block naming `document` plus
`start_byte`, `end_byte`, `start_line`, `end_line` and an optional `excerpt_hash` —
all-or-nothing, checked by `akr check` (AKR-S022) — never by chunk id, because chunk
boundaries are allowed to move and provenance is not.

**Context.** A first attempt at ingesting an outside advisor report fragmented it into one proposed record per heading, kept only the first paragraph of each, and let the original be deleted: the detail was gone, the fragments were never reviewed, the graph did not connect them, and the work board filled with unadopted headings. Markdown is the right format for the first reading of a rich technical audit; the question was what AKR should hold instead, and how a record should point at the part of a report it was written about.

**Consequences.** Sparse adoption is the default: a record exists only because the project adopted, rejected, deferred or decided to track something in the material, and everything else stays readable in the report rather than becoming unreviewed project state.

**superseded by** `@akr.decision.external-sources-immutable-library/2`

## akr.decision.git-facts-batched-by-ledger-file

### Revision 1 — Git facts are batched by ledger file

`active` · `@akr.decision.git-facts-batched-by-ledger-file/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/session.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/git/**"`, `path "crates/akr-mcp/src/tools.rs"`

Git remains the snapshot and acceptance-provenance boundary, but knowledge writes must not derive one record at a time by spawning Git history queries for every revision. Compute definitional last-change facts in batches by ledger file, parse each historical file version once, and avoid a second Git-enriched session open merely to format a successful write response. Lifecycle state, notes, verified_by links, unrelated records in the same file, and commits that only alter those bookkeeping fields do not move a record's definitional last change. Recorded as D-036.

## akr.decision.inherited-facts-not-conclusions

### Revision 1 — Inherited facts are cheap; inherited conclusions are not

`proposed` · `@akr.decision.inherited-facts-not-conclusions/1` · scope `all`

Moving work between agents is one mechanism, akr handoff, in three levels inherited by reference and never copied: a project capsule derived from the checkout (toolchain, layout, commands, namespaces, what is authoritative and what is generated), a session capsule (HEAD, the ledger revision, the user's request verbatim, constraints, baselines, the rendered session head), and a packet (role, task, scope, what is known, what must not be repeated, what to return). Results are packets too, carrying findings, evidence, changes, uncertainties, follow-up and coverage. Four modes decide what a child sees of the parent's judgement and nothing else: worker discloses the parent's notes, scout, reviewer and advisor withhold them until a recorded reveal. The task may be narrowed but never replaced, because the session's verbatim request renders above the assignment. Scope defaults to the whole project. A child opens its packet instead of calling knowledge.start, and akr start says so when a session is open. Recorded as D-041, amending D-040.

**Context.** D-040 built an advisor packet: one bounded object for one second model. Delegation to ordinary subagents is the same shape and the larger waste, because five of them re-derive the toolchain, the module map, the build commands and the current plan five times over, and do not always arrive at the same answer, which costs more than the tokens because the disagreements are invisible. Asking what actually differs between an advisor, a scout, a worker and a reviewer gives one answer: how much of the parent's judgement the child may see. That is a field, not a subsystem, so D-040's advisor packet was a special case wearing the name of the general thing.

**Consequences.** Inheritance by reference is the load-bearing choice: copying a capsule into each packet would have been simpler and would have produced five snapshots drifting apart silently, which is the failure the capsules exist to remove. The three withholding modes are mechanically identical on purpose, differing in the contract each states and what each is asked to return, because three disclosure policies to make them look distinct in code would have been decoration. Coverage is the field that pays for itself: without it, five capable agents told to review a project all check the same obvious doorway, and the aggregate reports as untouched only what some child named as unopened and no child read, because silence is not evidence of absence. The MCP catalogue gains fourteen tools, reaching thirty-seven, which is a large addition to a list documented as closed and earns it because a subsystem a child must use instead of knowledge.start has to be fully reachable over MCP. The agent-facing guidance collapses from four files to one, at four lines, and the Claude skill file is deleted rather than trimmed, because a second place to learn the same thing is a second place for it to be wrong. AKR cannot see process ancestry so it cannot enforce the child rule; it reports it as a line in the session head rather than a diagnostic, the standing scratch has under D-036.

## akr.decision.mcp-budgeted-and-instrumented

### Revision 3 — The MCP surface is budgeted and instrumented

`active` · `@akr.decision.mcp-budgeted-and-instrumented/3` · scope `path "crates/akr-mcp/**"`

knowledge.get takes summary|body|canonical, defaulting to body. MCP results without a caller-selected output budget are measured across both text and structured halves. A result over its per-tool hard limit must still return a useful first page or compact preview and an actionable continuation that preserves every required argument; wholesale replacement with a truncation notice is forbidden. knowledge.start and knowledge.context are internally budgeted: when budget_tokens is explicit, context or handoff assembly owns that budget and the MCP adapter must not discard the assembled result behind a smaller fixed ceiling. Search continuations page deterministically through ranked results rather than merely retrying a smaller first page. knowledge.validate pages diagnostics by limit and offset, defaults to a bounded first page, and reports the total and next offset. knowledge.evidence_add_many accepts 1–100 ordinary evidence payloads and commits all of them through one atomic validation pass or none; single writes and bulk writes reload only the written workspace state for their response rather than reopening a Git-enriched session. Authoring schemas state that topics are single segments and distinguish depends_on prerequisites, including completed planning prerequisites, from derived_from provenance. akr-mcp --surface read omits the write tools; --accounting appends one JSON line per call. The server publishes its vocabulary version and reports a workspace disagreement as a named skew. Recorded as D-034 and revised after collated field evidence showed wholesale withholding made the tools unusable.

**supersedes** `@akr.decision.mcp-budgeted-and-instrumented/2`

## akr.decision.mcp-envelope-verified-against-real-clients

### Revision 1 — The MCP envelope is verified against real client generations, not against our own reading

`proposed` · `@akr.decision.mcp-envelope-verified-against-real-clients/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-mcp/src/protocol.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-mcp/tests/conformance.rs"`, `path "docs/08-mcp.md"`, `path "scripts/verify-mcp-conformance.sh"`, `path "tools/mcp-conformance/**"`

The MCP wire envelope is verified in two layers, and neither subsumes the other.
`crates/akr-mcp/tests/conformance.rs` checks every response against closed sets written
out by hand, with no dependency of any kind; `tools/mcp-conformance/` drives the server
with three major versions of the rmcp client library at once, from outside the
workspace, run by `scripts/verify-mcp-conformance.sh` and by CI. The first layer is the
only one that catches an omission -- a supported protocol version quietly missing is not
a malformed response and no client will ever report it. The second is the only one that
catches a client generation becoming stricter than the one before it, which is how every
defect here has actually been found. A published JSON Schema is not a third option that
replaces either: the 2026-07-28 schema types `resultType` as an unconstrained string, so
it admits the exact value that broke every tool call.

**Context.** Three defects shipped through the same gap: `supportedProtocols` on a discovery result, a discovery result shaped like an initialize result, and `resultType: "tool"` on every tool this server has. None produced a JSON-RPC error. Each was a successful response a strict client could not deserialise, which is worse than a refusal, because a client retreats from an error and can only give up on a malformed success. They were invisible for a fortnight for a reason worth recording: nothing in this server regressed. Claude Code made 586 successful tool calls between 4 and 17 August, and Codex 0.147 called eight knowledge tools on 13 August, against a server already emitting `resultType: "tool"` -- rmcp 1.7 has no concept of the field and serde dropped it. Codex 0.149 bundles rmcp 3.1.2, which types results by it, and every tool call stopped working on 21 August with the server unchanged. The threat is client strictness drifting under a server that never moved, and rmcp alone has published 62 versions across four major lines.

**Consequences.** `tools/mcp-conformance` is excluded from the workspace and keeps its own lock file, so `cargo test` is unchanged and `akr-mcp` keeps its zero dependencies, dev-dependencies included. The cost is a second Cargo project and about 150 crates that CI builds and no shipped binary links. Older client generations are kept in the matrix deliberately as the control: a defect that fails on 3.x and passes on 1.x has reproduced the real event rather than merely failing.

## akr.decision.one-writer-at-a-time

### Revision 1 — The write pipeline claims the workspace, and refuses a source that moved under it

`proposed` · `@akr.decision.one-writer-at-a-time/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-core/src/ops/**"`, `path "docs/07-cli.md"`

Step 0 of the write pipeline takes an advisory lock on `.akr/cache/write.lock` through the operating system's own file locking, held from before the ledger is read until every touched file has been renamed into place. Writers therefore queue and all of them succeed. Immediately before the renames, every file about to be replaced is re-read and must still hold the bytes step 1 read; a disagreement is `AKR-C034` and writes nothing.

**Context.** The pipeline is a read-modify-write and only its renames were atomic, so two processes that both read before either wrote each held a ledger that did not know about the other's record, and the second rename discarded the first while both reported success. Six concurrent `akr papercut` processes landed two records (@akr.observation.concurrent-writes-are-silently-lost). Several agent hosts against one workspace is the normal way this ledger is used. `base_rev` did not cover it: that is optimistic concurrency over one key's head revision, and a newly proposed key engages it nowhere.

**Consequences.** Two mechanisms rather than one, because a lock binds only the processes that take it. The lock lives on an open file handle, so the kernel releases it when a process ends however it ends — no stale lock to reap, no timeout to tune — and it costs no dependency, `std::fs::File::lock` being stable. The re-read is the backstop for what the lock cannot cover: an editor, a `git checkout`, or a filesystem whose locking does not work, where the guarantee degrades from `writers queue` to `a racing writer is told` rather than back to silent loss. The critical section holds no git and no index work, so a queue of agents moves through it in milliseconds each. Measured: sixteen concurrent proposals of distinct keys, sixteen landed; with the lock disabled, three landed and the other thirteen were refused rather than lost.

## akr.decision.papercut-subject-and-collation

### Revision 3 — A papercut says what it was about

`active` · `@akr.decision.papercut-subject-and-collation/3` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/write.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/papercut/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/render/papercuts.rs"`

A papercut has an optional about slot naming what the friction was with when that is not its owning project. By default akr papercut collate gathers only sister papercuts whose about matches the namespace receiving the master record; --about selects other subjects and --all explicitly takes every subject. The command counts filtered records, carries every selected statement in full, and names only contributing projects. Every historical collated slot contributes to the dedup set even after its master becomes terminal: resolving or withdrawing a master never makes the absorbed source reports new again. PAPERCUTS.md renders a collation as one summary line and gives subject-bearing papercuts their own heading. Recorded as D-033 and revised after terminal masters replayed resolved reports.

**supersedes** `@akr.decision.papercut-subject-and-collation/2`

The command counts filtered records rather than dropping them silently, carries every selected statement in full, and names only contributing projects in the master title. ### Revision 1 — A papercut says what it was about

`superseded` · `@akr.decision.papercut-subject-and-collation/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-core/src/papercut/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/render/papercuts.rs"`

A papercut gains an optional `about` slot naming what the friction was with, when that
is not this project. `akr papercut collate --about <subject>` gathers only the sisters'
papercuts aimed at one subject, and counts what the filter left behind rather than
dropping it silently. A collation carries each source papercut's full statement, not a
truncated title; PAPERCUTS.md renders a collation as one summary line and gives
subject-bearing papercuts their own heading. Recorded as D-033.

## akr.decision.post-commit-validation

### Revision 1 — Post-commit identity is graph-based and co-committed evidence is current

`active` · `@akr.decision.post-commit-validation/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-core/src/render/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/resolve/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/validate/**"`, `path "docs/16-change-protocol.md"` · topic `post-commit-validation`

Generated views embed the source-graph hash but no Git commit hash. A commit hash
cannot be embedded in bytes that participate in that same commit; Git maps the stable
graph to snapshots through AKR-Graph trailers and knowledge.start reports HEAD.

Passing evidence is current when it descends from the verified record's last content
change, or when the evidence record and verified record were introduced or changed in
the same commit. Co-commit identity proves the evidence was authored for the prepared
snapshot without weakening rejection of genuinely older evidence.

**Context.** The previous banner made every clean post-commit build differ only by the unknowable future commit hash. Evidence observed against the prepared parent similarly became stale when the implementation and its completion landed together.

**Consequences.** Generated projections are stable across the commit boundary and remain traceable by source graph. Acceptance freshness preserves D-016 while explicitly supporting the staged-tree workflow documented by the change protocol.

## akr.decision.query-words-dirty-tree-ancestry

### Revision 2 — A query is words; a dirty tree is a fact

`active` · `@akr.decision.query-words-dirty-tree-ancestry/2` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/session.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/git/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/store/search.rs"`

akr search escapes ordinary query terms and joins them with OR by default, with BM25 ranking records that match more terms first; raw FTS5 remains behind --fts and is never exposed over MCP. This makes multi-word natural-language orientation recall useful records even when no single record repeats every task word. AKR-G004 is exempt from strict promotion under D-024. ancestry_over uses one cat-file --batch-check and one rev-list --topo-order instead of a comparison sort whose comparator forked git. Recorded as D-035 and revised after field reports of silent multi-word misses.

**supersedes** `@akr.decision.query-words-dirty-tree-ancestry/1`

## akr.decision.revision-and-replacement-contract

### Revision 1 — Revision and replacement contracts are explicit

`active` · `@akr.decision.revision-and-replacement-contract/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/src/write.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/context/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/ops/**"`, `path "crates/akr-mcp/src/tools.rs"`, `path "docs/04-references-and-versioning.md"`, `path "docs/07-cli.md"`, `path "docs/08-mcp.md"`, `path "docs/09-context-assembly.md"`

An explicit lifecycle state on a revision is authoritative and lands on the successor.
A content-only revision of sealed knowledge starts proposed so changed content is
accepted deliberately. Context accepts bare keys, @keys, and a pin to the current head;
it rejects historical pins and anchors with retrieval guidance. Replacing a different
key is a two-step contract: first propose the complete same-kind replacement, then
atomically attach its pinned supersedes edge and retire the old head.

**Context.** Reconciled papercuts showed that CLI and MCP advertised overlapping reference and replacement forms but applied different lifecycle defaults and recovery paths.

**Consequences.** Callers can predict successor state and reference handling. Different-key replacement requires one extra authoring call, but the final graph transition remains atomic and never constructs an incomplete replacement implicitly.

## akr.decision.revision-is-not-redefinition

### Revision 1 — Revising a record is not redefining it

`active` · `@akr.decision.revision-is-not-redefinition/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-core/**"`, `path "docs/**"` · topic `freshness-definitional-change`

Revising a record is not redefining it. `last_change` compares definitions across the
revision boundary: the projection it hashes drops the revision number and a
`supersedes` naming an earlier revision of the same key, on top of everything D-029
already removes, and the history walk continues past the commit that introduced a
revision into the history of the revision it was revised from. A `supersedes` naming
a different key is a real editorial statement and is untouched, and every definitional
change D-029 keeps still moves the gate.

**Context.** D-029 narrowed "content change" to what a record requires, so completing a milestone would not strand the evidence that closes it. That reaches only the in-place case, and D-015 makes a sealed record uneditable — revising it is the only way to change it. Revision n+1 did not exist before the commit that wrote it, so its last definitional change was that commit by construction and every citation it carried was instantly too old. Retargeting a check at a measurement that had already landed un-satisfied the check, with no way to re-land it: a fresh observed_at would have to name a commit that does not exist yet, and duplicating the evidence duplicates a measurement nobody re-ran.

**Consequences.** A revision that changes nothing definitional preserves its predecessor's last_change, so acceptance verdicts survive a lifecycle edit, a note, and a plain retarget. This can lower an existing last_change, so a ledger built before and after this change can disagree about which commit that was; it is a projection difference, not a diagnostic. Byte reproducibility is unaffected — the computation stays a pure function of the repository and the ledger. The D-015 seal still hashes the whole revision.

## akr.decision.search-refreshes-disposable-index

### Revision 1 — Search refreshes its disposable index before querying

`active` · `@akr.decision.search-refreshes-disposable-index/1` · scope `path ".akr/cache/index.sqlite"`, `path "crates/akr-cli/src/commands.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-mcp/**"` · topic `record-search-cache-refresh`

akr search and knowledge.search must rebuild a missing or source-graph-stale record index from the currently loaded ledger before querying it. This cache refresh may occur as a side effect of a read because the cache is disposable and non-authoritative; it must not modify records, the lock, or generated views. When --no-rebuild is set, a needed refresh fails with AKR-I031 and leaves the cache untouched.

## akr.decision.start-collates-session-head

### Revision 1 — Start collates a validated session head

`active` · `@akr.decision.start-collates-session-head/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-cli/**"`, `path "crates/akr-core/**"`, `path "crates/akr-mcp/**"`, `path "docs/**"` · topic `session-head-briefing`

AKR start and knowledge.start automatically prepend a deterministic, bounded project
handoff assembled from the latest validated ledger snapshot, reachable AKR-linked Git
history, live planning heads, review state, and any valid working-tree ledger overlay.
Task-specific search remains in the same response, and canonical authority remains in
records and Git rather than the projection.

**Context.** Agents currently spend the beginning of sessions searching for whichever planning record is newest. A collated session head should provide the recent work focus and all outstanding branches before deeper task-specific retrieval.

**Consequences.** Start becomes Git-backed while search remains ledger-only. The handoff is an ephemeral projection, not a new record kind or committed generated file.

## akr.decision.write-answers-for-what-it-introduces

### Revision 1 — A write answers for what it introduces, not for what it inherits

`active` · `@akr.decision.write-answers-for-what-it-introduces/1` · scope `path "crates/akr-core/src/git/mod.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/ops/mod.rs"`, `path "crates/akr-core/src/validate/rules.rs"`, `path "docs/07-cli.md"` · topic `write-refusal-scope`

Step 3 of the write pipeline compares rather than asserts. It derives the resulting ledger's diagnostics and, only when there are any, restores the pre-edit text of every touched file, re-derives, and takes the difference as a multiset keyed on code, rule, subject and message, never on span. A diagnostic this write introduced refuses it, nothing written and the working tree byte-identical. One the ledger already had does not, and is reported as a note naming the count and the codes.

**Context.** "Validates the resulting ledger" had been implemented as "the resulting ledger has no errors", which refuses every write into a ledger that is already invalid — including the write that would repair it, since each repair must first produce a ledger with none of the other faults in it. V-025 arrived on 2026-08-23 and judges history, so raw-autotune was left carrying 35 unfixable AKR-T023s and Lege-ecosystem 20 more plus 8 AKR-R022s, with hand-editing a .akr file the only escape and the protocol forbidding it. An agent hit it and wrote its findings into a Markdown file instead, which is the outcome the ledger exists to prevent. A promise that cannot survive its own violation is a latch, not an invariant; the one worth keeping is that a write never makes the ledger worse.

**Consequences.** A broken ledger is repairable one record at a time through the sanctioned path. The intake guarantee is unchanged: evidence is born verified at revision 1, so a citation made today is always a new subject, introduced, and refused on all four write routes. A write can now land into a ledger that does not build, and akr build, akr validate and akr check are unmoved and still fail on the whole ledger, so nothing here hides drift. Two extra derivations are paid only on the path that was about to fail anyway. Two diagnostics were reworded alongside it: AKR-T023's help now names dropping the artifact slot, the only repair left once scratch has been pruned, and AKR-R022 distinguishes evidence that genuinely predates a record's last definitional change from evidence observed on a branch this history does not contain — the ancestry fact being a topological order that cannot tell the two apart, so a separate reachability fact answers it. That moves wording only; across all thirteen AKR workspaces the diagnostic profile is byte-identical before and after.
